opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that they're really two halves of one project. The "Circuit Tracing" paper is the methods paper. It's where we lay out the tooling: how we train a replacement model, specifically cross-layer transcoders, that approximates the original model's MLP computation with features that are much more interpretable than raw neurons. Then we describe how we build attribution graphs from that replacement model for a specific prompt, so you can trace which features influenced which other features, all the way from the input tokens to the output. A big part of that paper is also being honest about the limitations: where the replacement model diverges from the real one, the error terms, the fact that we freeze attention patterns, and so on. It's basically "here's the microscope, here's how it works, and here's where it's blurry."

"On the Biology of a Large Language Model" is what happens when you point that microscope at an actual model, in our case Claude 3.5 Haiku, and go looking at a bunch of interesting behaviors. That's where you get the case studies: multi-step reasoning, where you can see the model actually compute an intermediate fact internally, like going from "Dallas" to "Texas" to "Austin." Planning in poetry, where it picks the rhyming word ahead of time before it writes the line. Multilingual circuits that share language-independent features. How it does addition, hallucination and refusal mechanisms, jailbreaks, and cases where its stated chain of thought doesn't match what it's actually computing.

The analogy we kept coming back to is biology. You need both the instrument development and the actual biology. Neither one is that useful alone. A method with no interesting findings is hard to evaluate, and findings without a clearly described method are hard to trust or build on. So we deliberately wrote them as companion pieces. If you care about how we know what we claim to know, read the methods paper. If you want to know what's going on inside the model, start with the biology paper, and then hopefully it makes you curious enough to go check the methods.

r001.rationale: It describes “Circuit Tracing” as the methods paper that lays out how the replacement model and attribution-graph tooling are built.

r002.rationale: It says “On the Biology” applies that microscope to Claude 3.5 Haiku to investigate mechanisms behind behaviors such as reasoning, planning, and multilingual processing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that one is the method and the other is what you find when you actually use the method.

The Circuit Tracing paper is the tooling paper. It's about how we build what we call attribution graphs. The basic idea is that we train a replacement model, where we swap out the MLP layers of the model with a sparse, more interpretable layer, so instead of these dense neurons that are polysemantic and hard to read, you get features that mostly correspond to a single concept. Then, for a given prompt, we can trace how those features interact with each other across layers and tokens, and build a graph that shows which features influenced which, and ultimately how the model got to its output. A lot of that paper is about the details: how you train the replacement model, how you handle attention, how you prune the graph down to something a human can look at, and how you validate that the graph is actually telling you something true about the underlying model rather than just about the replacement model. That last part is important, because the replacement model is an approximation, and so we do a lot of intervention experiments where we go back to the real model and perturb features to check that the story holds.

The Biology paper is, in some sense, the fun one. It's where we take that microscope and point it at Claude 3.5 Haiku and just look at a bunch of behaviors. The analogy we kept coming back to is biology. If you build a new microscope, you can write a paper about the optics, but the thing people actually care about is what cells look like. So in the Biology paper we go through case studies: multi-step reasoning, where you ask about the capital of the state that Dallas is in, and you can see the model internally represent "Texas" before saying "Austin." Poetry, where the model plans the rhyme word ahead of time before it writes the line. Multilingual circuits, where you see shared conceptual features across languages. Addition, medical diagnosis, refusals, jailbreaks, and cases of unfaithful reasoning where the model's chain of thought doesn't actually match what's happening inside.

So the relationship is really that they were written together, and they were meant to be read together. We split them because the methods details would have made the case studies unreadable, and the case studies would have made the methods paper enormous. But honestly, the method only matters because of the findings, and the findings are only credible because of the method. And I'd add that a theme in both is being upfront about limitations. The replacement model doesn't capture everything, attention patterns are taken as given rather than explained, and there are plenty of prompts where the graph is just too messy to interpret. We tried to be clear about where the microscope is blurry.

r001.rationale: It describes Circuit Tracing as the tooling paper and explains how the method builds attribution graphs to trace internal feature interactions.

r002.rationale: It says the Biology paper uses that microscope to examine Claude 3.5 Haiku’s behaviors, with case studies showing internal representations and circuits behind them.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two halves of the same project. “Circuit Tracing” is the methods paper: how do we build tools that let us trace some of the internal computation a model uses to produce an answer? “On the Biology of a Large Language Model” is about applying those tools and asking, what can we learn about how the model works?

The biology analogy is useful because we’re taking something complex and studying particular mechanisms within it. We’re not claiming to have a complete understanding of the model. We’re trying to move from observing its behavior to forming hypotheses about what’s happening internally, and then testing those hypotheses through interventions.

So one paper lays out the approach and its limitations, and the other shows the kinds of scientific questions that approach lets us start exploring.

r001.rationale: It calls “Circuit Tracing” the methods paper about building tools to trace the model’s internal computation.

r002.rationale: It says “On the Biology of a Large Language Model” applies those tools to learn how the model works and study particular mechanisms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two complementary pieces of the same effort. “Circuit Tracing” is about the methodology: how do we trace the computations inside a model and build a useful picture of how it arrives at an answer? “On the Biology of a Large Language Model” is about applying that methodology: what do we discover when we use those tools to study the model?

The biology analogy is helpful because having an instrument doesn’t mean you already understand the organism. You use it to make observations, form hypotheses, and then test those hypotheses. And those investigations also tell you where your instrument is limited and what you need to improve. So there’s a feedback loop between developing the tools and doing the science.

r001.rationale: The response describes tracing computations and building a picture of model reasoning, but does not say the paper explains how the tool itself is built.

r002.rationale: It says the paper applies the methodology to study the model, but does not clearly identify investigating mechanisms underlying model behavior.
